newsitem.title: ITALY: Sale of Olivetti PC decision greeted with relief.
newsitem.headline: Sale of Olivetti PC decision greeted with relief.

text.p: The announcement by Italian information group Olivetti on Monday that it is selling its ailing personal computer business to a group of domestic and international investors was greeted with relief by industry-watchers.

Olivetti's chief executive Roberto Colaninno told a news conference at the company's offices in Milan that Olivetti stood to gain 250 ($158.5 million) to 300 billion lire from the sale of its PC division to a newly-constituted company called Piedmont International.

But analysts said they would like to know more about Edward Gottesman, the U.S. lawyer who played a key role in bringing together the investors from Italy and abroad who are backing the Piedmont venture.

Institutional investors who hold a majority of Olivetti's stock have been pressing it for many months to sell the troubled PC division, which they see as a millstone dragging down the loss-making information technology group's performance.

Gottesman's venture capital company Centenary Group will be a shareholder in Piedmont, to be chaired by Italian industrialist Gianmario Rossignolo, who currently heads Electrolux of Sweden's Zanussi white goods unit in Italy.

"Under the right direction and with the right management we are confident that the (PC) business can have a future in Europe," said Gottesman who added that Rossignolo was chosen because of his experience in turning round the Zanussi business which Electrolux bought in 1984.

Olivetti shares, which were suspended from trading on Monday pending the announcement, had risen recently in expectation of the sale. They closed at 672.8 lire on Friday and some analysts said some investors may be tempted to take profits and sell the stock when trading resumes on Tuesday.

Gottesman told the news conference that he had ties to Olivetti's former chairman, Carlo De Benedetti, who through his CIR company is the largest single shareholder in Olivetti with around 15 percent.
"I have known Carlo De Benedetti for more than 20 years and I have done legal and other work on behalf of Olivetti," Gottesman told the news conference.

De Benedetti helped rescue Olivetti in the late 1970s and turn it into a successful PC maker in the 1980s but investors have criticised him for failing to act decisively when the group plunged into loss at the beginning of the 1990s.

"People said they had to sell the (PC) business and there is certainly some relief that they have sold even if it is to someone who appears to be close to the group," said Mike Pacitti, a London-based analyst with HSBC James Capel.
"One of the things people are going to want to know about him (Gottesman) are his relationship with Olivetti," he added.
The exact price of the sale, to be based on the net asset value of the PC business, will not be settled until the deal is finalised by the end of February.

Olivetti will be paid 80 percent of the sale price at the end of February with the balance payable in instalments. It will also receive a share of any profits made by Piedmont in the first three years of activity.
"They didn't tell us the whole story," said another London-based analyst who asked not to be named. "There are still questions to be answered."

Gottesman said that information about Piedmont International's backers would be revealed "in due course" although he said Rossignolo had been given the option to acquire a shareholding in the business.
Despite the sale of the PC business -- a deal which Olivetti said should bring in 250 to 300 billion lire -- Olivetti will retain close links through a 10 percent stake in the Piedmont venture.

Olivetti will also retain ownership of a PC plant at Scarmagno in Northwest Italy, currently employing 1,600 people, which it will lease to Piedmont for four years. Olivetti will also license its brand-name for PCs to Piedmont for 20 years. $=1,570
